prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "DEERE & CO" (ticker DE), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "DE", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Deere & Company
markets: Large farm equipment (high-horsepower tractors, combines, sprayers, planters)
Precision agriculture technology and farm software
Small tractors, turf and lawn equipment
Construction, forestry and road-building equipment (incl. Wirtgen)

mission.statement: We run so life can leap forward.
mission.source: John Deere's stated 'higher purpose', published in its 2020 Sustainability Report release; its website now headlines 'We innovate on behalf of humanity.'
mission.plain: Deere wants its machines to help people grow food and build things so everyone's life gets better.

about.plain: Deere makes the big green-and-yellow John Deere tractors, combines and sprayers that farmers use to plant and harvest crops. It also makes lawn mowers, small tractors, and machines like bulldozers and loaders for building roads and buildings. More and more of its machines have computers, cameras and GPS so they can steer themselves and spray only the weeds. It also lends money to customers so they can buy its machines.
about.customers: Farmers, landscapers, homeowners, construction companies, road builders and loggers, mostly buying through John Deere dealers.
about.everyday: Much of the corn, wheat and soybeans in the food you eat was planted or harvested with a John Deere machine.

money.plain: Large tractors, combines, sprayers, planters and precision tech
Loaders, excavators, dozers, road-building and logging machines
Small tractors, riding mowers, golf-course and utility equipment
Loans and leases to customers and dealers

money.part: Autonomy, smart spraying and farm software
money.plain: Self-driving tractors, See & Spray weed cameras, Operations Center data

result.summary: Deere has a wide moat in farm equipment built on the John Deere brand, the industry's densest dealer network, a huge installed base and a lead in precision-ag technology that ties machines, data and software together. Its pricing power held up even in the FY2024-FY2026 farm downturn, though results remain highly cyclical and right-to-repair rules and tariffs chip at the edges.

pricingPower.evidence: Production & Precision Ag reached a 26.1% operating margin in FY2023 on price realization; even with FY2026 large-ag industry demand guided down 15-20% in the US and Canada, Deere still expects positive price realization of about +1.0% in PPA, +1.5% in Small Ag & Turf and +3.0% in Construction & Forestry (Q3 FY2026 release).

moats.evidence: The green-and-yellow John Deere brand, founded in 1837, is the most recognised name in farm machinery and commands premium prices and resale values.

Farms run whole fleets on Deere's JDLink telematics and John Deere Operations Center (over 520 million engaged acres per the Q3 FY2026 call), so field data, displays, guidance and dealer service relationships make switching costly.

Nearly 1.2 million connected machines feed agronomic and machine data that improves Deere's software and attracts third-party app integrations, while a large installed base supports the deepest used-equipment and parts market.
With FY2025 equipment net sales of $38.9 billion, roughly double AGCO's and CNH's industrial sales, Deere spreads R&D, precision-tech development and distribution costs over far more units.
Rural dealer territories support only a few full-line dealers, and Deere's dealer network typically holds the strongest location in North American farm country.
Deere's shift toward tech subscriptions and 'solutions as a service' is something rivals can attempt, though smaller peers lack the R&D budget to match it quickly.
Decades of combine and sprayer engineering plus in-house computer-vision (Blue River Technology, acquired 2017) and autonomy (Bear Flag Robotics, 2021) know-how underpin products like See & Spray.
Its independent dealer network is a valuable semi-exclusive asset, but Deere has no exclusive patents or resources that rivals cannot work around.

customers.evidence: Farmers are famously loyal to 'green' equipment and Deere's large-ag share and premium resale values reflect it, though right-to-repair anger led to a $99 million class-action repair settlement and a July 2026 FTC settlement requiring Deere to share repair tools for 10 years.

talent.evidence: Deere is a long-standing Fortune World's Most Admired company (No. 1 in Construction and Farm Machinery for six straight years to 2023, No. 2 on the latest list) and appears on Forbes' America's Best Employers lists, but it has had labor strife such as the 2021 UAW strike and recent layoffs.

product.evidence: Deere leads in precision tech: See & Spray customers report over 50% herbicide savings, factory-installed autonomy-ready and guidance systems are standard on its large tractors, and roughly one-third of North American sprayers on order carry See & Spray (Q3 FY2026 call).

competitors.name: CNH Industrial N.V.
competitors.note: Case IH and New Holland tractors, combines and precision tech; CASE construction equipment.

competitors.name: AGCO Corporation
competitors.note: Fendt, Massey Ferguson and Valtra tractors and PTx Trimble precision ag, strongest in Europe and South America.

competitors.name: CLAAS KGaA mbH
competitors.note: Private German maker of combines, forage harvesters and tractors.

competitors.name: Kubota Corporation
competitors.note: Compact and utility tractors, mowers and compact construction equipment.

competitors.name: Mahindra & Mahindra Ltd.
competitors.note: World's largest tractor maker by units, strong in India and US compact tractors.

competitors.name: Caterpillar Inc.
competitors.note: Construction equipment: loaders, dozers, excavators, motor graders.

competitors.name: Volvo AB (Volvo Construction Equipment)
competitors.note: Excavators, wheel loaders, articulated haulers and road machinery.

competitors.name: Hitachi Construction Machinery Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: Excavators; former Deere-Hitachi excavator partner in the Americas until 2022.

competitors.name: SDF Group
competitors.note: Private Italian maker of Deutz-Fahr, SAME and Lamborghini tractors and combines.

competitors.name: The Toro Company
competitors.note: Golf-course, commercial and residential turf equipment.

competitors.name: Husqvarna AB
competitors.note: Residential and commercial mowers and forestry tools.

competitors.name: Doosan Bobcat Inc.
competitors.note: Skid steers, compact track loaders and compact tractors.

competitors.name: Daedong Co., Ltd. (Kioti)
competitors.note: Kioti compact and utility tractors in North America.

threats: Prolonged farm downturn: FY2026 US and Canada large-ag industry sales guided down 15-20% and South America down 15-20%.
Tariffs: about $1.1 billion of direct FY2026 tariff expense (about $750 million net of refunds) and a roughly $1 billion run-rate in FY2027.
Right-to-repair: the July 2026 FTC settlement forces Deere to give farmers and independent shops dealer-level repair tools for 10 years, weakening dealer service lock-in.
Lower-cost rivals such as Mahindra, Kubota and Chinese makers in small tractors, and CNH/AGCO precision-tech catch-up (PTx Trimble).
Farmer pushback against tech subscription pricing and data ownership.
Credit losses at John Deere Financial if farm incomes fall further.

ceo.name: John C. May
ceo.background: Bachelor's degree from the University of New Hampshire and MBA from the University of Maine; former KPMG consultant, joined Deere in 1997 and served as CIO, head of China operations and president of Worldwide Agriculture & Turf.

c1.evidence: Deere leads precision agriculture and farm autonomy, a fast-growing field, but its core tractor and combine industry is mature and cyclical.

c2.evidence: Farmers choose Deere for its brand, dealer service, resale value and integrated tech stack (Operations Center, See & Spray, autonomy), advantages built over decades that are hard to copy.

c3.evidence: John Deere's green-and-yellow tractors and 'Nothing Runs Like a Deere' slogan are known well beyond farming, and it is the default leader in North American large farm equipment.

c4.evidence: Its higher purpose, 'We run so life can leap forward', and its focus on feeding a growing world are repeated by management, though the company is also run with tight financial targets such as 20% mid-cycle operating margins.

c6.evidence: “reliable, iconic, American, expensive”: the impression is mostly positive and nostalgic, tempered by right-to-repair criticism from some farmers.

c7.evidence: Rising global food demand, labor shortages and data-center and infrastructure construction support a large market, but it is cyclical rather than a fast secular-growth market; Deere targets a 10% net sales CAGR by 2030.

c8.evidence: Deere is extending into autonomy, computer-vision spraying, construction tech (SmartGrade) and software subscriptions, but stays within equipment-related markets.

m1.evidence: John May set the 'Smart Industrial' strategy and the 2030 'Leap Ambitions' around automation leading to autonomy, a clear technology vision for farming.

m2.evidence: May is a career Deere executive (joined 1997) who invests through the cycle in technology, but he is a hired steward rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: Deere stresses customer outcomes, but May's tenure included the 2021 UAW strike and later layoffs and right-to-repair disputes with customers.

m5.evidence: Under May Deere bought Bear Flag Robotics (2021) and pushed in-house software and AI, building a more tech-driven culture.

m6.evidence: May is not an engineer, but as former CIO he is closely involved in Deere's technology and digital strategy.

m7.evidence: No scandals are tied to May, and he speaks about feeding the world sustainably, but there is no clear evidence of a mission beyond running the business well.

m7b.evidence: No record found of John May giving a commencement address at a top university.

m8b.evidence: May keeps a low public profile typical of industrial CEOs.

m9.evidence: Under May Deere posted record net income of $10.166 billion in FY2023 and kept FY2025 net income at $5.027 billion in a deep farm downturn.

m10.evidence: Deere is known for cost discipline through cycles, but there is no notable reputation for frugality at the CEO level.

c10.evidence: Deere machines help produce food, fiber and fuel and build infrastructure worldwide, with nearly 1.2 million connected machines in use.

p2.evidence: Building reliable combines, autonomous tractors and real-time computer-vision sprayers is very hard and essential to world food production.

f1.evidence: Net sales and revenues rose from $35.5B (FY2020) to $61.3B (FY2023) but then fell to $51.7B (FY2024) and $45.7B (FY2025).

f2.evidence: Equipment gross margin rose from 24.3% in FY2020 to 27.6% in FY2025 and operating margin from 12.1% to 13.2%, but both are well below the FY2023 peak of 32.1% and 21.2%.

f3.evidence: Equity was $27.99B at Aug 2, 2026, but consolidated debt of $63.8B against $10.3B cash is high, though most of it funds John Deere Financial's customer loans.

f4.evidence: Operating profit rose from $4.3B in FY2020 to $6.0B in FY2025 (peak $13.0B in FY2023), while operating cash flow was flat at $7.48B and $7.46B.

v1.evidence: Deere is widely seen as the best full-line large-ag brand for its tech, dealer support and resale value, but CNH, AGCO (Fendt) and CLAAS offer strong competing machines.

v2.evidence: Deere ranks No. 2 in Construction and Farm Machinery on Fortune's latest World's Most Admired Companies list and has appeared on Forbes' America's Best Employers, but it is not a top-tier tech-style employer brand.

c5.evidence: If Deere vanished, millions of farmers and their dealers would lose machines, parts, service and financing, disrupting food production across North America and beyond.
